utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, ma'am. All the accused are here. Mr. Meek is absent as per agreement. So is Mr. Bourgon. The rest of the Defence teams are here. The Prosecution teams, Mr. McCloskey, Mr. Thayer, Mr. Vanderpuye. All right. Any problems with interpretation or with the monitors, let us know, okay? I think -- I see that the witness is not in the courtroom. Are there preliminaries that you would -- yes, Ms. Condon?

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. All right. Yes, Ms. Condon.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Can I first of all indicate to the Court that the motion that I referred to yesterday evening has in fact been filed this morning and a copy was -- a courtesy copy was provided to the Court yesterday. So I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you for having provided our staff the courtesy copy because it helped us prepare of course and enabled us to come with a decision in due course this morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the ballpark has changed somewhat this morning in terms of the witness Rutten is concerned from the Popovic perspective. And that's because at 11.30 yesterday evening, we received a note of a proofing session in which the witness first of all was obviously shown the photo in question that is the subject of our motion, but also, and I'm just reading from the proofing note directly; what it says is: "When he was asked what he meant when he testified that the man looked not like a plain soldier, he responded that the man clearly appeared to be in command and have authority." Now, in my submission, Your Honour, this is new evidence insofar as the case against Mr. Popovic is concerned. It is -- puts an entirely different taint on what otherwise would be an identification which was still obviously of significance to our case but combined with this assessment, as to a position of power, in my submission, that places us at a severe disadvantage in terms of being able to deal with this witness in any proper form, either today or tomorrow, and I've already foreshadowed that we certainly weren't in a position to deal with him immediately for cross-examination. The other aspect that in my submission it raises is that this is a witness that surely should be examined in full rather than a 92 ter witness which the Prosecution have made the application for him to be, simply because this is evidence of sufficient significance insofar as our case is concerned that it really doesn't warrant either procedure, 92 bis or 92 ter. And I also would indicate, and this is a matter that was raised in the motion generally, in my submission, Your Honour, it's simply unacceptable that the Prosecution would provide this information to us at 11.30 prior to this witness giving evidence. That is contrary to any principle of an accused having a fair trial, and I just have to register, certainly, my objection, because it is just unacceptable. And I make this submission that this is simply too important for this witness to proceed today. They are my submissions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Ms. Condon. Who's is going to respond to that? Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can stay where you are. Unless there is an objection, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Is this all right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm fine with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. The proofing notes absolutely were sent out at that hour. That is simply by virtue of the fact that again this issue arose Sunday. The witness at issue is full time military duty. He arrived in The Hague last evening at 8.30. I was sitting with him by 9.00. By 10.00 we were done. By 10.30 I'd finish escorting him to the hotel, and by 11.00 these proofing notes were disclosed in considerable detail to Defence counsel. That was just the hour that it got completed. It's an unfortunate consequence of the way this issue unfolded. Now, with respect to the nature of the evidence, Your Honours, this is perfectly consistent with the role that is, is alleged that the accused Popovic has played throughout the indictment and throughout the pre-trial brief, notwithstanding the fact that it wasn't specifically mentioned as a particular act or conduct in either document. It is the Prosecution's position that this is evidence that is consistent with other evidence which the accused has been placed on notice about. It is evidence that the Prosecution firmly believes can be adequately prepared for in time with this witness's appearance here at this time. This is -- this is not surprise evidence in the nature of the evidence. Obviously the notice is an issue but I believe that we've cured that. The proofing notes that I had to provide last night were a natural consequence of having to sit down and show this witness the photograph, as my learned colleague has acknowledged, and it does not provide anything substantively different from the testimony that is already in the Krstic transcript. I think the implication is clear when you read the transcript when he says, "not a plain soldier," he's referring to somebody that appears to be in command. I asked him that specific question so it was a clarified issue and I put that in the proofing notes. There are other material in the proofing notes - I won't burden the Court with the details - but it's nothing that is substantially different from what's in the Krstic testimony, what we have alleged his role to be throughout the indictment and the pre-trial brief. I would also add that to this day this witness doesn't know the name of the individual he identified in the photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Thayer. Incidentally, let's do some lateral thinking about all this. Assuming for the time being, we obviously haven't decided it as yet, but assuming that this witness will be a ter -- 92 ter witness, how long do you anticipate the additional in chief to last?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I think about 15 to 20 minutes, Your Honour. It's a limited group of questions and frankly this photographic testimony will be two or three questions, max, itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Again, assuming that everything will go according to what would be scheduled, if all objections are turned down, which they aren't at the moment, Popovic Defence team, how much time do you reckon you would require with this witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is a difficult --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: -- question simply because there is the issue with relation to the identification which would take a significant amount. I would say two hours to two and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Two hours. Beara team?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we join obviously the motion by our colleague, and on principle I would say no cross-examination because it comes at such a late hour. However, if the Court and given the last few weeks with the witnesses that you've given me some latitude on, at most it would be 15 minutes. But I truly believe that the Prosecution is trying to bring witnesses in at the late hour and they should have their evidence. They should identify which witnesses are specifically against which accused, as they have done in some instances, and I object to the practice and it doesn't include me or involve me specifically or my client; however, I think the practice is specifically what I'm objecting to, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Thank you. Nikolic Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Defence of Mr. Nikolic will take no more than 20 minutes; however, we do endorse the submission of the Popovic Defence in the light of the submission of the Nikolic Defence. This conversion of the witness statements really does constitute admission of new evidence. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As for the cross-examination of Mr. Rutten who is coming, I believe that we will have at least one and a half hours for him and we would also like to back up Popovic Defence in their motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And further there is another issue raised yesterday by Mrs. Fauveau, and I believe that she will address the Trial Chamber regarding this, another issue, and it has to do with the disclosure of some documentation related to Rutten, to Mr. Rutten, which is in Dutch and which we still haven't received any --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It was raised yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is indeed a problem. Madam Fauveau, first, how much time you require for cross-examination, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, 30 to 45 minutes. As to the problem raised yesterday, I would like to say that all the Defence teams have joined my application. I would also like to react to what the Prosecutor said. He said that we could cross-examine as to certain topics and that the witness could be brought back for further examination as to items covered by this. But we don't know what is in the statement and if we start cross-examining a witness today, to continue later on, that would be a waste of time and I don't think it is very useful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You also have been told by Mr. Thayer that it is a -- practically repetition of what is contained in the other statement but in any case, I haven't been able, like you to read it at all because it's in Dutch. Mr. Josse or Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Approximately 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Mr. Haynes or Mr. Sarapa?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: 20 to 30 minutes and we stand foursquare with Ms. Condon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we have five hours 30 minutes estimated cross examination of this witness. Plus 30 minutes or 20 minutes. So actually estimated six hours. Now, we have three hours 30 minutes tomorrow, and we still have this witness for another hour, hour and a half, at least. So that would leave us with about two hours today. We can make it. We can make it. Technically, because of course we have to discuss the issue raised by Ms. Condon and also the issue raised by Madam Fauveau. We'll come to that back to you, we'll come back to you on that later on after the first break. Okay. Any further preliminaries? I think we can bring the witness in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Witness answered through interpreter].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir, and welcome back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are going to continue and finish with the cross-examinations. So yesterday we had finished with the Nikolic team, Defence team, examination. Now it's the Borovcanin turn, Borovcanin's team's turn to cross-examine you. Mr. Lazarevic is lead council. Go ahead Mr. Lazarevic. We are in open session. Any time we need to be in private session, please let us know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour, and I'll have it in mind all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Let us not repeat some of the mistakes that we committed yesterday. Please make a pause after the -- I finish my question before providing your answer so that everything goes into the transcript and the transcript is clear and unambiguous. During these proceedings, we've had occasion to see a number of notebooks and intercepts, as we call them here, and we saw certain markings of these notebooks, type 21, 22, 23 or 21/1, 2, et cetera. My question would be: Were you the one who ascribed numbers to those notebooks or was this done in the platoons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot really specify, but I believe that we took a chronological order of numbers. At the time when we handed them over to the ICTY, it was a strictly confidential notebook number 1, strictly confidential notebook number 2, et cetera, et cetera, and this is how we marked them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us that these markings were put before handing them over to the ICTY or in the -- or in 1995? Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that these markings were done in the period when we were supposed to hand them over to the ICTY, if we are talking about the same markings, the same numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I presume that this is the case. During your testimony, you mentioned the term Paket service or Paket communication service. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Since we are laymen, we do not understand this very much, could you understand -- could you explain what this is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the north and south facility, we did not have the same technical possibilities and capabilities in both cases. From the north, we had a wired connection and radio communication. With the southern facility, we had only Paket radio service, which means that the reports that had been collated at such facilities were coded, packaged and sent through the ether to the command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Paket radio communication is a computer-protected information that is sent over the radio waves. Would this be in laymen's terms what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is nothing laymen's about it. You put it very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We have a piece of information examined by this Tribunal that towards the end of 1993, such a Paket radio communication was established between the 28th Brigade in Srebrenica and the command of the 2nd Corps in Tuzla. Well, now, for me to provide the grounds for this question, I presume that you know which the 28th Brigade is. It was in Srebrenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It was part of the 2nd Corps, which was headquartered in Tuzla and which you were part of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to ask you given that you were in the 2nd company --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps we should move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: We can now turn to a different topic. In response to the questions put to you by John Ostojic yesterday about what you said in your examination-in-chief, you said that in relation to certain persons, there existed already dossiers in which you wrote some of their features, their voices, and some of their personal features. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And I suppose that that was done on the basis of long term work and a large number of intercepts, that that was used to compile a dossier, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct. I came to this unit in February of 1995 and there already existed a certain database for certain persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The fact that many operations officers there heard the same voice several times was also used as a basis for identifying the person whose voice they heard, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Operations officers wrote down names and last names of persons who either used a code name or directly identified themselves, and you can see, if you go through the transcripts, wherever they were not sure of the identity of the person, they would denote that person either with an X or a Y.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in this: If an operator heard some voice for the first time, a voice not heard before, could such an operator be able to identify that person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally don't think so, but he could always write that he supposed that the identity was such and such.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: There are situations in which certain assumptions of operators were recorded, as you said, but that does not necessarily imply that they were correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Assumptions were confirmed at a higher level. They did not necessarily need to be correct, but were taken at face value, so that was one of the positions taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: When you said "at a higher level," what would that higher level be? Could you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday that the data gathering is quite a broad process. Intercepts are just one aspect of it. It was our duty to provide the data that we possessed in that field, and then data were collected from other fields as well. And all of that went to the intelligence department of the command of the 2nd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: To simplify, so the higher level that you spoke of was the intelligence organ of the 2nd Corps, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in terms of my unit, that was the higher level.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. Just a few more things to conclude: You served in the JNA. You worked for many years on this type of work. Are you familiar with the term "operations masking"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: You became familiar with it back when you were with the JNA, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber what that term denotes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simply speaking, it means that by pronouncing certain phrases and using certain expressions, you are masking the situation on the ground in order to mislead enemy units.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. It's Madam Fauveau now, who is defending General Miletic, who will be cross-examining you. How much time do you require, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try to finish by the break, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we move to private session, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But what do you mean to say by if the document is not shown to the witness? Because that's what I have in the transcript. You mean to say if it is not broadcast, if it's shown to the witness only but not outside this courtroom? All right. Okay. So we understood.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, is it right to say that in paragraph 2, or, rather, tell us first, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is this an order that you gave on the 22nd of June 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right now, I can't tell you exactly. As I told you, there were many such orders. Based on what I can read here, I can conclude that this is a squad or a section which was established pursuant to the order of the command of the 2nd Corps and at that time they were attached and they worked pursuant to the directives of the 2nd Corps command. If I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it an order that you gave to your unit that was stationed in the south, according to which you asked them to follow --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I guess the nature of the objection is, Mr. President, that if it is counsel's position that this is an order that the witness gave and it's reflected in the document, perhaps the entire document should be shown to the witness. Maybe there is a signature or some other indication on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we go by your objection and I think Madam Fauveau would concur with that, too. I think we need to show the witness the entire document to give him the opportunity to be able to give a more comprehensive answer or more reasoned answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that we should show the document on page 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think we've seen enough. Madam Fauveau, you may proceed with your question, either repeating it or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we go back to page 1, paragraph 2, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, now that you've seen this document, can you tell us if, in fact, this is an order pursuant to which an information was given to the section that was in your southern area but also information -- in this document, we saw that the order was given to jam enemy communications; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, you're right. This is my order which was produced based on the order that had arrived from the 2nd Corps. Initially I said that we had some amplifiers that were not very powerful so jamming them did not produce much effect, but the command of the 2nd Corps instructed us to do that kind of work nevertheless.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You're saying that this jamming did not really -- was not really efficient but were they done? Did you actually carry out the jamming procedure?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did do the jamming, but I personally do not think that they produced much of an effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can you tell us if the people who were assigned to those positions, to the -- who had the task to jam the communications between people in the Republika Srpska, those same people, were they working in the intercepting within the -- were they intercepting communications? And the technique that was used to jam conversations, was that technique different than the one used to intercept conversations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You've told us on the 27th of November, page 24 of the transcript, that your units were checking frequencies from 200 to 900 megahertz. Is it possible to check frequencies that were above 900 megahertz?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. By saying so, I mean that we transformed that information into speech, into voice signal that can actually be listened to.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What device were you using to convert high frequencies to audible frequencies to the human ear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try to explain that. There were three steps in that procedure. The first step was to procure a device whose band could be expanded, band of frequencies. The second step was to manufacture a converter, which was a smallish device, so that this high frequency could be converted to voice signal. And this converter had a preamplifier, so these three steps allowed us to listen successfully to the communications up to 900 megahertz.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What devices were you using to catch frequencies between 266 and 630 megahertz?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were mostly ham radio devices, RM 3.000, Collins, JVC. These manufacturers are well known here in the western market as well, but as ham radio devices, they had a very narrow band within which they could communicate. That was the problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: While we are still talking about the equipment that your section had to the south and the north, was there a difference regarding the quality of the equipment? The equipment in the north was it better than the equipment that you had in the south or vice versa?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you that the equipment was similar. If we took some ham radio equipment from Banovici and sent it to the facility in the south and then found similar equipment in another municipality, such as Srebrenik or Lukavac and send it to the north.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... quality of the equipment in the north and in the south?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it exact to say that the two places had difficulty to get electricity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. However, we had additional power supply in the form of generators. The ones in the facility in the south had remained from the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You've said yesterday, on page 22 of the transcript, that your UHER equipment was very good. Is it right to say that it would happen that these equipment or that that equipment could actually break from time to time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I said that during that period of time, the equipment that we had was considered of high quality. Furthermore, the JNA used that equipment in their wiretapping centres.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it exact to say that those devices could break down from time to time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Normal procedure requires, or rather normal procedure -- it is normal for the equipment which is constantly used to occasionally be out of order.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it exact to say that you had difficulty to obtain pieces, to change, to put in those devices?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true, but we had people who were very enthusiastic, who could produce something out of nothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it true to say that you did not have maintenance products to maintain that equipment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: During that period of time, and during war, we did not have anything. We had a short supply of everything, including the spare parts for UHERs.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it exact to say because you didn't have maintenance products and maintenance parts, that the quality was diminished, that you didn't have such a good quality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to say, because very soon thereafter, we found certain sources. By that, I mean the radio station in Tuzla, where they had a lot of equipment that we could use for spare parts. The quality of the recording mostly depended on the reels which had been used several times.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown 5D153, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, can we say that this is a report coming from the southern area, written on the 13th of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would like you to take a look at paragraph 2, please. In this paragraph, we can see that there were some problems with a UHER which was out of use at that time, is that right to say? It's in the first sentence of paragraph 2 that we see this.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will provide a very clear answer to this question. Such reports were sent to me and I would forward them to the 2nd Corps command, for the reason to refresh or replenish our stocks. We would repair these breakdowns very quickly. But we wanted something in writing to be sent to the command although we knew that we could receive little or nothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And is it right to say that the last sentence of this paragraph states as follows: "That this is why more and more conversations were being completely incomprehensible, so wiretap became totally incomprehensible or taping of the conversations became incomprehensible"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That statement can be taken as true but as I said, to get something, and we will some reserves, we had to exaggerate to be able to receive at least something.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I understand very well what you're telling us, sir, but can you tell us today with certainty --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have I think two objections to make with respect to I guess the question and answer, with respect to the exhibit they have just been displayed. One is that I believe my learned counsel referred to the last paragraph in the document, and I believe translated that last sentence, maybe I'm incorrect, but she referred to taping and/or listening and I'm not sure that the document reflects that. And secondly, I'm not clear on whether or not the translation of intercepts is being converted into wiretaps or some other expression. I think there is a clear distinction between what an intercept is of a radio communication and a wire tap and I'm concerned that that may lead to some confusion with respect to what the transcript later bears out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you wish to comment on that, Madam Fauveau? We are not in a position to make an assessment. We need feedback from the interpreters on this or anyone else who is, for that matter, following the proceedings, maybe in B/C/S. Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm understanding you but we don't have an interpretation in English now. And for the benefit of anyone who doesn't understand French, if you don't mind repeating, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I was not referring to the last paragraph but to paragraph 2. But for the sake of clarity and to make it easier, it's a short paragraph. The easiest thing might to be read it out in B/C/S for it to be interpreted by the certified translators and interpreters. They are the most competent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But in the transcript indeed we have in line 7 on page 23, your question as being, is it right to say that the last sentence of this paragraph, but you're referring to paragraph 2, okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exactly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We need to -- did you have that in mind, Mr. Vanderpuye or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes. I do stand corrected. The substance of if, however -- the substance of the objection remains the same, which is I believe that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Wiretapping or intercept?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's correct. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So the only thing, other thing, we need to clear up, unless you intend to clear it up with your next question, Madam Fauveau, is this question of whether we are having the correct translation of the words you are using in French into English. I wasn't following you in French when you asked the question. So I'm not in a position to know whether we have got the right interpretation or not, the correct interpretation or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think the best thing would be to read the text again, as it stands in Serbo-Croat, and it might be necessary to read the entire paragraph for the text to be understandable. It won't take too much time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Agreed, agreed. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. "What is being done to have more regular supplies for small spare parts for UHERs? One UHER has a dysfunctional drive disk so it's completely out of repair and out of use. What we need is regular supplies of spare heads, new tapes and rubber bands, and we cannot even obtain alcohol for the cleaning of magnetic heads. And this is the sure reason that more and more we have recordings of conversations which, when played back, are hardly or completely unintelligible."

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, I've just read out a passage. Did it indeed have to do with the recording of conversations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't know whether this is clear enough now or whether the Prosecutor would seek other elements on this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'll accept the translation as was, as I heard it, any way, and I have no other objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Madam Fauveau, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, if I understood you properly, you sometimes overstated the problems you encountered but isn't it fair to say that it would happen that you would send the reels with the recordings to the -- your higher command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: They, therefore, could ascertain the quality of the recording, couldn't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In essence, yes, but we did not send tapes from which we could not play back voice information. We whinged, we sought, but we did have something up our sleeve in reserve as any diligent service, but we wanted the command to provide more to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know when the platoon for electronic surveillance was established in the northern facility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I already said, this was before my arrival to the service. I cannot remember precisely, but I think they were there in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yesterday, you testified that the unit in the northern facility covered the area between Doboj and Zvornik, and you said that it was the Posavina area. Is it fair to say that this very same area was also covered by a unit of the 21st Division that were located in the same place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct when you're talking about the points of the compass but the interpretation is not correct. The northern facility covered the area from Doboj to Zvornik, and the unit from the 21st Division covered the area of Posavina, which overlapped 20, 30 per cent, with the 21st's area of responsibility in terms of deployment of its units and brigades. We had a platoon of communications and monitoring for the 25th Division and of course there is some overlap in surveillance because we are talking about air waves and communication can come from any direction. But the main area of responsibility for the northern facility was to cover area left of Doboj and right of Zvornik a supplementary task was to help the southern facility and vice versa in case there were some major operations in their areas of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... area you have just defined between Doboj and Zvornik, was it exactly the same as the one covered by the units of the 21st Division that were located in the same place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which area was established through an order and given to the 21st division but in terms of military hierarchy, you know and you must know, that a division is subordinated to a corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the objection to the question is simply that I believe it had already been answered in the prior -- with respect to the prior question and it's repetitive and I would just object on that basis. Obviously, it's already been answered but I think twice is probably enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is different. It is different. Because the emphasis now is on the strict difference that there is between Doboj and Zvornik. So the area covered earlier was more concentrated on the units of the 21st Division, as I see it. Anyway, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: With regard to the northern facility as such, your unit, your platoon, and the unit of the 21st Division, would they exchange, swap, information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a normal process to exchange information and data. Our task and their task was, if there were no activities in said area, or no activities in the area of responsibility of the 21st Division, they would turn their antenna and monitor communications in the south. You must know that apart from the platoon within each division, we had squads at brigade levels and at any rate they could detect activities but such squads did not have such a level of equipment that they could monitor in the way that a -- division level and corps level units could.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I am going to put it to you directly. The members of your unit in the northern facility, did they know of intercepts done by units of the 21st Division?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Members of our unit did not know about these intercepts, for the reason that intercepts from the 21st Division were sent to the command of the 21st Division, and after processing these, their commander sent the same information to the corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did the members of your platoon know of intercepts by the DB unit that were positioned in the same northern facility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, no, but I cannot exclude mutual conversation which was aimed at support and help. State Security Service was mostly interested in the intercepts of conversations of civilian or political structures, but they, to justify their existence, most probably monitored military communications as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did it happen that you received from your platoon in the northern facility reports regarding intercepts done by the DB?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot exclude this possibility but it would be a very rare occurrence.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: How could you receive intercepts done by DB?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: How is it possible that you would receive conversations that were intercepted by the DB unit? On which channels did you get this information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would come to us in the following manner. They would provide their report to our unit, and we would package it and forward it to the corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: So there was, indeed, an exchange of information inasmuch as the DB would send to your northern facility the intercepts they had done?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already stated "very seldom," for the very simple reason. One person cannot produce a volume of work greater than six or seven people could, and very rarely did they come up with something that we had not already obtained.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You said on the 27th of November, page 44, that a signals platoon was in the northern facility and that the said unit used specific equipment or a room in which the head of the platoon and the person working there were allowed to enter. Is it right to say that the DB personnel were allowed to enter that room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but I can freely tell you that DB members could not enter the premises of my KZ or cryptographer service or my units.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we move to private session because I'm about to mention a name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move to private session nor a short while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: On the 27th of November you stated that the commander of the platoon was the first filter in data analysis. Could you tell us what that amounted to, this first filtering level on information or data?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will try to make it understandable. Commander sits with a number of people together in one room and everybody is working. If all routes are occupied, he would determine the priorities. And that would be the first filter: What is to be monitored and what is not to be monitored, exclusively for the reason of limited technical capabilities of the equipment at our disposal.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And the commander of the platoon had he been trained in data analysis?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course he would be informed because everybody sitting in a single room and talking now I can hear this and I can hear the other person. They would perform analysis to transcribe faithfully or as faithfully as possible the conversations intercepted.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: There may have been a problem in the interpretation. I'm going to repeat: The commander of that platoon, had he been trained in analysing data?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe he was in the -- within his purview.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: On the 27th of November, page 40 of the transcript, you said that you were mainly interested in the contents of conversation, that you did not insist so much on the people speaking. Would you allow for the possibility that there were some mistakes in identifying the speakers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our task, and I will reiterate, is correctly to interpret what was said and as -- and for the conversation to be transcribed on paper or in -- to be keyed into computer, as was. We do not -- we were not interested in their names. We drew conclusions on the basis of the forms filled in, on the basis of introductions of participants in conversations, or some other indications. No person would be ascribed a name if they had not introduced themselves or if there were no indications as to the identity of the person. We would put X, Y, even in cases where there were many indications among our men that this could be a certain person.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... intercepts were not of the same relevance.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's only normal.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You would receive reports from the northern and southern facilities. Did they distinguish between relevant and not so relevant intercepts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Their task, as I said, was to forward the reports as they were to the superior command, but if there were some reports that were urgent in terms of shelling, in terms of bombing, then this delay could not happen and they had a duty to notify immediately.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: The urgent reports regarding bombing or shelling, did they bear a special mention, such as priority or urgent?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I can remember, there were markings urgent and priority, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And the marking was the same or there was no distinction between urgent and priority? Was one more urgent than the other?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In essence, both such types of reports had the same or similar weight. The only difference was the time of response. As I already said, urgent, if they were planning to shell Tuzla from Ozren so that alarms can be sent, and priority meant that that information should be heeded but there would be more of a lag -- time lag between the sending and receiving.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You forwarded or you handed over various material, reels and copy books, between 1998 and 2000. Do you know when the ABiH received a first request from the OTP for the handover of such documents?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I just see in the translation a reference to copy books, and I just want --.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Apologies by the interpreter, we meant notebooks.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, do you know when the ABiH received a first request by the OTP regarding this material?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will respond very briefly. You should ask that somebody from the federal Ministry of Defence or from the joint command. I only know when I received my superior officer's orders and this is when I started doing that job.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You forwarded or handed over certain reels among this material. Where were they kept before they were handed over to the OTP?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: These tapes were safeguarded within the unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you say "unit," could you be more specific? Where was this unit located?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, it was done in the northern facility.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, in the Krstic case --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it was in closed session so I'd like to read out a paragraph from that transcript. Can we move to private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. Let's move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And we'll have a 30-minute break starting from now. Thank you. One moment. I seek the cooperation of the Defence teams. We have a new motion from the Prosecution regarding protective measures for the December witnesses. We are dealing with witnesses number 69, 134, 136 and 65, for whom a pseudonym, visual and image -- and vocal, and voice distortion are sought, and 157, 77, and 81 for whom pseudonym and image distortion are sought. The most important thing is that witness 69 in particular, although scheduled to start on the 1st of December won't be able to start on the 1st of December but he will certainly -- he will certainly start mid-next week. So if you could let us have your position, joint position, or whatever, latest Monday morning or Friday, this Friday or latest Monday morning, we would appreciate that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are not sitting on Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No we are not sitting on Friday but they can inform our Senior Legal Officer and we'll receive the communication. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, just before the break we were talking about archiving. Is it right to say that all official documents were archived in Sarajevo as of 1996?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, I'm not authorised to release such information, but all of this went to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And what about the books and all the notebooks that remained in the northern part, the northern facility? All those documents remained there; is that right? Those are the official documents?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you gave the OTP those documents, did you inform the OTP that those are not official documents?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody ever put such a question to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that the previous answer was not recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are right. And the question was,"And what about the books and all the notebooks that remained in the northern part, all these documents remained there; is that right? Those are the official documents?" What did you -- what was your answer to that question? I'm asking you again because it didn't show up in the translation, in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Notebooks and tapes, let me repeat once again, were accidentally maintained. The official document is the written report, and the official documents are actually tapes that were contained in the intelligence department. When the representatives of the ICTY expressed interest, at that time we were not considering in terms what is official, what is not official. We simply looked for original sources and I think that I was clear enough in explaining this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. I think it's clear enough. He's making a clear distinction between what is official and what is not official documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown the document P2312, 2312?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You've told us yesterday, sir, that the reports that were coming from the northern facility to the southern facility, that those reports were sent to your unit. Can you explain to us why is it that on this report we see that the person who was to receive the document was the 2nd Corps intelligence organ?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already explained that the reports arrived in parallel to the unit and to the intelligence section of the 2nd Corps where there also existed an encryption department. They would only change the heading, so that above the line where it says, "intelligence section of the 2nd Corps," they would put a different text, PEB Company, and they would send it forward because, to people receiving it, it was important to know where such reports originated.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: To be clear, all the reports from the northern facility and the southern facility were sent automatically to the intelligence section of the 2nd Corps and to your unit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And the report that we have before us is the report that was sent to the 2nd Corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You've told us yesterday that the initials that we see here under the text designate a person, the person who would usually send the report as well as the person who transcribed the conversation. Did every report contain an initial like this?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the witness mentioned the name of the northern facility. It is not written down in the transcript but he did say it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I think we need to redact also only the audio part, and that should be enough. Thank you. Careful; we are in open session. Yes, Madam Fauveau, thank you for pointing that out.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, when a report contained many different conversations, these initials were supposed to be put on top of each conversation or only at the end of the report?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first initials, as you can see here, al ways the same. That person stayed there for 10 days in a shift. If there were more reports and if these reports were produced by the same person, that it was sufficient for that person to put his initials at the bottom of each report.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown page 2 of this exhibit, please? Page 10, please, excuse me. Maybe there was a mistake in interpretation. I was mentioning page 10. Could the witness be shown the end of the page, so the bottom part of the page?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir , is it right to say that no initials appear on this page?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown the next page, please? Could the document be, yes, raised a little bit between the two conversations? That's right. This place.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, here we do not see any initials. We do not see an initial at the end one conversation, for instance.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we turn to the next page, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And at the end of this conversation, we also do not see an initial; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please take the following page? Could we please scroll the document down?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: On this page there are no initials as well; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like the witness to be shown the next page.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, it is the end of the report and we still do not see an initial. When you would receive such a report without an initial, was this a regular occurrence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was a typical situation. As I said earlier, putting initials down was not a legal requirement. We asked for that in order to recognise the work of certain servicemen, so there were very few people who put down their initials and those are the people who worked 24 hours in ten-day shifts and it was very easy to establish based on that who produced what report because we had adequate notations in the notebooks. So we could trace the work of a certain person; however, putting down the initials was not a legal requirement.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would like to take page 3 of this document. I would like this page to be shown to the witness. Sir, is this a conversation that was intercepted by the DB?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And this conversation was sent from your section, from the northern facility; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know how members of your section got in possession of this document or more generally speaking this DB document? How did they get this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I have said, the state security, the DB, was tasked with monitoring civilian communications. This one here is a typical military communication and they simply gave this communication on a diskette. Our person repackaged it and sent it to Sarajevo. You can see that in the right corner it says, "Very urgent."

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, you've told us yesterday that generally speaking, as an average, there were 25 to 30 conversations during a day, between 20 and 30 reports were drafted in the course of one working day; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have said that it all depended on the traffic, density of traffic on that day. There were days when we had one, two or three reports, and that did not depend on us.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And on the 14th of July 1995, according to you, was this a day with a lot more conversations or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From my point of view, I can tell you that there were more conversations than typical, than usual.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And is it normal that under these conditions 16 reports would have been sent?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The number is completely irrelevant. It can contain more conversations that were recording on more channels or it can contain one single conversation recorded on one channel. And that could be the entire report. It depended on the speed of typing of the operator doing this. Whenever there was a need to send a report, he would produce a short version or, if he had sufficient time, he would produce a longer version.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... say that problems regarding dates would occur on these reports?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In such a situation where people worked around the clock, 24 hours a day, such mistakes were possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you recall that an order was given in the month of August 1995, pursuant to which the date was to be automatically written down above each conversation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't answer. Wait one moment. Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. It just appeared to me that part of the previous question was missing. I didn't hear it in the translation and I don't see it on the transcript. I don't know if maybe counsel could either repeat the question or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Either counsel or myself. I don't see the reason why counsel is speaking French. I don't imagine that the witness is following in French. And still there is some overlapping. Still there is some overlapping. I've noticed it and even Judge Prost raised it with me earlier on. There is some overlapping so I don't know what the cause of it. Perhaps we can go back, if you could repeat your question, kindly repeat your question, please, Madam Fauveau, and then the witness will try to answer it again.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, the counsel needs to wait for the English interpretation to conclude before asking the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was entirely my fault the missing portion of my question was, is it right to stay that problems regarding dates would occur in these reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And what was your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that in such an environment, it was normal for mistakes to occur. Whenever you have a team playing, you will always expect them to play even better. That's the essence of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Incidentally, Ms. Fauveau, I don't know in you're following the transcript in English or not but the interpreters have pointed out that it would be preferable and much easier for them if you waited until the English translation is finished before you proceed with your questions in French. And that's according to them the reason why we have had some problems. All right? I'm sure you can do that because the transcript is -- will be scrolling in front of your eyes, so ...

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really have to follow the transcript because I have to see also what is going on with French because I'll enter into collision with the French language as well. So I really have to follow the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall an order from the 20th of August 1995, in which an order was given that a date should be written on top of each conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right now I do not remember that order. There were many orders. However, such orders, in such a form, typically came from the intelligence department. As I have said to you the purpose was to improve the work. That was the only goal.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown Exhibit 5D117, please? Would it be possible to show the witness the bottom of the page, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, do we see your name at the bottom of this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could the witness be shown what is written on top of the page? Mr. President, could we go into a closed session for just a few moments while I discuss this document with the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown 5D131, the cover page more specifically? This is notebook 00778815. I don't know whether the Prosecutor has the notebook. It might be good to put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, whilst this is being done, whilst you're receiving the original, could you tell us whether this notebook that you can see on the screen is like the notebooks you would use in your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally think that this is one of the notebooks used by the members of my unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, you stated that you would receive the notebooks from various sources. Isn't it fair to say that part of them would come from the humanitarian aid destined to the children?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea about that, really.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No further questions, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Josse or Mr. Krgovic? I don't know who is --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We are not asking any questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the Borovcanin -- Pandurevic Defence team have already finished their cross-examination. Is there re-examination, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No, there is not any re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So witness, we don't have any further questions for you, which means that your testimony comes to an end here. Our usher will escort you out of the courtroom and our, the rest of our staff will assist to you facilitate your return back home. On behalf of the Trial Chamber, I wish to thank you for having come over and also extend our best wishes nor a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We can now proceed with the tendering of documents. Mr. Vanderpuye goes first. Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We would like to tender first the transcript of his prior testimony, which is P02309. The pseudonym sheet P02310.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Both of which will be under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, please. Also we would like to tender -- just bear with me for one moment. I'm trying to get a document that I need myself. Also like to tender P01067. It's a copy of the record of transfer of archival material from the 2nd Corps to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Stop for a moment because we'll try to economise on time as much as we can. I suppose this list that is been plead available to all the Defence teams.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you confirm that, that you have had this list made available? You have therefore the list of all the documents that the Prosecution seeks to tender. Are there any objections from any of you, any of the Defence teams, with regard to any of these documents? Yes, Ms. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. If this is the document submitted to us on the 28th of November, given that there were two documents in circulation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. This is -- it's not dated and I don't have the date on it. Yes, it is dated in the bottom, 28th of November. It ends with PIC 00050.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it there are no objections so all these documents are so admitted and they will be attributed the P number or the exhibit number that we have there indicated on this sheet, which I'm handing to the registrar. That is all?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes. The only thing I wanted to add is perhaps for the Court to consider admitting P01075 under seal and also P01071 under seal to the extent that they bear identifying information concerning the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which ones again, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think that is necessary because he was actually asked whether he recognises his own signature or whether he prepared those documents. So those two documents, I suppose, there is no objection on any of the Defence -- on the part of any of the Defence teams. I hear none. So those two documents will be kept under seal. All right. So I take it that the Popovic Defence team would like to tender some documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. We've submitted our list of documents put forward to be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I take it that the Prosecution has a copy of this list. They don't seem to have a copy of the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Sorry. In response to your question, I don't believe we have a copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So now that you have more or less gathered what the practice will be, if in future you could make sure that the list is distributed both to your colleagues, and I'm addressing you because it happens to be you. I'm addressing everyone. Both your I have it will leagues and the Prosecution so we facilitate the process. I'll go through it very quickly. The there are six documents. They are 1DP1068, 1DP1069, 1DP1071, 1DP1072, 1DP1075, 1DIC00049, as described in the piece of paper which I am handing signed by me to the registrar. Yes, but it is IDP1071. That would be the same one. This would be the same one and they would need to be under seal as well. All right? [Trial Chamber confers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: These documents will be so admitted; however, in relation to 1DP1071 and 1DP1075, these will be kept under seal. I would also like someone to check whether in relation to the other documents, barring the last two, in other words, barring IDIC 00049 and the other one, which we haven't given a number as yet, archive notebook in part, just pages 0204 to 0384 and 0204 to 0722 to what is document bearing ERN number 02040772 to 02041112. The others, registrar, needs to check whether in any part of the witness's testimony there are references made to these documents which could expose his identity. I don't think there are but there may be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. It is only two pages. So in relation to item 6, the two pages from the archived notebook, it's only those two pages of course that are being admitted as a 1D -- Defence 1D exhibit and they will be given a number in due course. Any objection? I hear -- makes me feel like conducting an auction. No objection? No objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No, not at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So they will be so admitted. All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I ask the number 2, 3, 4 items are same documents as Prosecution documents, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, they are. We have an instruction to submit such documents in this way, even if they are included in the Prosecution's list of documents and to mark them in that manner, and this is what we've done. Of course, I will double check with my team but I think that we have abided by your instructions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. I think -- thank you very much. I think that before proceeding with the the next witness, you are all anxiously expecting our decision, Madam Fauveau. You have also some documents to tender?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, very much so. We have the list. You have the list, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And I can paraphrase it, summarise it, it's 5D152, 5D142 and 5D153, these being first list of members of the unit, second order dated 22nd June, and third document dated 13th July 1995 respectively. I'm handing a sleet to the registrar with my signature which indicates the ERN number of these documents. I thank you. Any objections? I hear none. So they are so admitted. Madam Fauveau. Can we proceed? No other documents to be tendered? Let's proceed now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Judge Kwon is rightly pointing out to me that it is preferable that the last document will be for the time being marked for identification pending translation thereof. As soon as translation is provided and goes in the record, then obviously the document is formally admitted. All right. Thank you Judge Kwon. That had escaped me. Let's come to our next business on our agenda. That's the next witness. Please comfort me when I say that this witness does not have any protective measures and that you're not seeking any protective measures for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. What is his current rank in the army, the Dutch army.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: He is a Major in the Dutch army, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. So this will -- what we are going to do now is we are going to hand essentially two decisions, both related to the Prosecution motion that I'm soon going to mention. The decisions -- both decisions are going to be oral. If needs be, we can then have them incorporated in a single or two written decisions but I don't think there will be a need for that. The Trial Chamber is seized of the confidential Prosecution motion to convert 92 bis witness Major Rutten to Rule 92 ter witness. This motion was filed on the 28th of November. That's yesterday. And basically what it amounts to is Prosecution seeking the admission of Major Rutten, who was Witness number 23, Major Rutten's evidence tendered pursuant to Rule 92 ter instead of the previous Rule 92 bis. Now, the Popovic Defence team made oral submissions yesterday, which were followed by a proper formal response filed -- and motion actually filed earlier on today, opposing the Prosecution motion. We have noted that in their response, and in their submissions, the Popovic Defence asserts, in trying to sustain their request that I will come to very soon, the Popovic team asserts that or submits that up until this time, there never has been any allegation made by the Prosecution that the accused Popovic was in the vicinity of the area of the "White House" on 13th July 1995, and that, I'm quoting, "In these circumstances it is unacceptable that three days prior to this witness giving evidence, the Defence is informed of the Prosecution's intention to rely upon this allegation." We have also noted that in their response, the Popovic team requests the Trial Chamber, first, to deny the motion and order that Witness number 23, that's Major Rutten, appear pursuant to Rule 92 bis. Second, to redact references in the transcript of that witness's prior testimony which affects the acts and conducts of the accused Popovic, and, third, to exclude the admission of document 65 ter number 1936, which we understand to be a photograph, and, last, in the alternative, in a subsidiary mode, to grant leave for further time to prepare -- further time to the Popovic Defence to prepare for their cross-examination of Major Rutten. During this morning's first session, Ms. Condon for the Popovic Defence team further raised another submission in support of her request, namely that they had received information that in the course of the proofing session of Major Rutten, he is reported to have told the officer of the Prosecutor interviewing him that it appeared to him that the person he identified, although not by name, in the photograph document 65 ter number 1936, was a person -- appeared to be a person in command and not a plain soldier. In our deliberations, we have considered the following. We first considered that on the 12th of September of this year, we handed down our so-called Rule 92 bis decision, in which the transcript of Witness number 23, that's Major Rutten, was admitted pursuant to Rule 92 bis(D), without the requirement of a witness to appear for cross-examination. That was our first decision. Subsequently, in reconsidering our decision, upon a request by one or more of the Defence teams, on the 19th of October 2006, we modified our previous decision, requiring Major Rutten to appear for cross-examination, and of course confirming the introduction of his previous testimony pursuant to Rule 92 bis(D). We have also taken into account during our deliberations that the photograph now in issue, namely document 65 ter number 1936, indeed was not admitted in our 92 bis decision, as it was not strictly speaking an exhibit that was admitted in the earlier trial as a result of witness number 23, that's Major Rutten's testimony, but was only referenced by the witness during that testimony. We followed up eventually in one of our decisions with a request to the Prosecution to also make available all these documents which included this particular document. That was made available not only to us but also to all the Defence teams.
