We have also considered that approximately 34 lines of the transcript of this witness's previous testimony described the actions of an individual appearing in this photo, which the Prosecution alleges to be accused Popovic. Now that the Prosecution proposes to admit that photo or to tender that photo in evidence, the relative written evidence in the transcript of the accused's prior testimony implicates directly the acts and conduct of the Accused Popovic as alleged by the Prosecution, with the consequent result that such testimony would no longer be appropriate for admission pursuant to Rule 92 bis because it goes to the acts and conducts of the accuseds. We have also considered that the Popovic Defence has had at its disposal this photograph, which they could relate to the witness's previous testimony upon reading the transcript of his prior testimony. Having considered further that the alleged role, and this answers the submission made by Ms. Condon earlier on this morning, we have considered further that the alleged role of the Accused Popovic during the alleged events in Potocari at the relevant time are clearly spelled out in the indictment and such an indication is by no means affected by the proposed testimony that the Prosecution seeks to adduce and that we considered would be absolutely nothing new as Ms. Condon seeks to make us believe. The Trial Chamber therefore, in considering the -- both the written and the oral submissions of the parties, we are persuaded that granting the Prosecution's motion will not prejudice the accused so long as the Popovic Defence team is accorded sufficient time to prepare its cross-examination of Major Rutten, and where sufficient cause is shown or will be shown in subsequent written or oral submissions, the same Defence team will be permitted to recall other witnesses for cross-examination. So our decision in relation to the motion and response by the Popovic Defence team is as follows: We hereby grant the motion of the Prosecution mentioned earlier on and order that the written evidence of Major Rutten, Witness number 23, is admitted pursuant to Rule 92 ter, provided that the provisions of Rule 92 ter, paragraph A, are duly adhered to and observed, and secondly, we hereby decide that on good cause being shown, the Popovic team - by the "Popovic team," Witness number 23, that's Major Rutten - will be required to be -- to appear for further cross-examination by that team at a later date to be decided by the Trial Chamber. I am now moving to the matter raised by Madam Fauveau, which has to my understanding been endorsed by all the other Defence teams. So I will be referring to it as your motion or your request, but the understanding is that it applies across the board to all the other Defence teams. We are referring to the same Prosecution motion. I don't need to repeat the substance of that motion. Earlier on this morning, Madam Fauveau submitted that one of the documents that the Prosecution has disclosed to the Defence teams in relation to the proposed testimony of this witness, Major Rutten, consists in a previous statement which he brought here with him to The Hague, a statement that purportedly he gave to the Dutch authorities and which is in the Dutch language, which is not a language with which the Miletic Defence team, and for that matter the other Defence teams, are familiar with. So it was suggested that in the absence of a timely translation of this statement, prior statement, of the witness, in a language which the various Defence teams can -- will be able to follow, they will not be in the position to conduct a full and well-informed cross-examination of this witness. As a consequence, Madam Fauveau, as endorsed by the other Defence teams, sought two things: Either the complete adjournment of this witness -- postponement of this witness's testimony to a later date when this is made available, preferably also with this witness coming forward to testify in full, without having resort to Rule 92 ter or Rule 92 bis, and also, in case such a request is not entertained by the Trial Chamber, to have the cross-examination delayed until this translation of this document has been made available. We do not consider that the fact this document has not yet been translated -- incidentally we are informed that it will probably be translated as early as this coming Friday, if not also tomorrow -- we do not consider the fact that this document has not been translated as an absolutely sufficient reason for the testimony of Major Rutten to not start and proceed as scheduled today. However, we also understand the problem that the absence of a translation of this prior statement may cause to the Defence teams, and so we are making a reservation that upon good cause being shown after a translation of the witness's prior statement to the Dutch authorities is provided to the Defence teams, Major Rutten may be required to appear again for further cross-examination by the Defence teams at a later date to be decided by the Trial Chamber. Incidentally, I'm also informed that not only will the translation be made available in time before the weekend, and we are not sitting on Friday, but that we have ensured that Major Rutten will also be available to continue his testimony on Monday morning. So we have tried to cover as much territory as possible to protect the various rights that you showed concern upon, but in the meantime we are going to start and proceed with Major Rutten's testimony. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any further matters you would like to raise before this witness walks in? Do you prefer to have the break now? I mean it's up to you. We can have the break now and continue in -- 30 minutes from now, or have him come in, start and break after ten minutes from now. It's whatever you prefer, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it would probably be smoother if we just take the break now and then bring him out and then really get on with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So that's it. Thank you. We'll have a 30-minute break now because of the redactions we had to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Major Rutten and welcome to this Tribunal. You're start to giving evidence or you have testified before. Our Rules require that before you do so, you enter a solemn declaration to the effect that in the course of your testimony you will be speaking the truth. The text is going to be handed to you now by Madam Usher. Please stand up, read it out aloud and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me explain very briefly what's going to happen. The testimony you gave in a previous case is going to be admitted in whole pursuant to a rule we have a new rule, that's Rule 92 ter, so you don't have to testify the whole thing again. However, Mr. Thayer, who will be leading you, will give you a summary of that testimony and then you will be asked a few questions, after which I will then pass you on to the various Defence teams. Now, one other thing before you start giving evidence is that one -- during your proofing session, you brought with you a prior statement that you gave to the Dutch authorities, which is in Dutch. You don't happen to have an English translation of it, by any chance, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you don't know if an English translation of it exists in the NIOD report or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We want to make sure Mr. Thayer that we don't have further complications arising out of this matter so we are giving you a specific instruction, directive, to have this statement or that statement translated into English. I think Madam Fauveau can live with that, too. Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I appreciate that, by no later than Friday noon. In order to make life easier for you, we are giving instructions to the registrar, or to the Deputy Registrar here, to copy and paste this part of our decision and have it transmitted to the registrar or the respective unit within the Registry that deals with translation. We find it absolutely unacceptable that in the Netherlands, in an institution where there are so many Dutch-speaking officers, this cannot be translated by noon. So the respective unit is to provide all its assistance to make sure that this is made available to the Defence teams immediately after noon on Friday. So this is your responsibility. Okay. Thank you. Having said that, I pass you on to Mr. Thayer. Go ahead, Mr. Thayer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Major.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Before we begin, we'll both be speaking English so it is especially important for each of us to leave pauses in between my question, your answer and then the next question so that we leave enough time for the interpreters to catch up so that it's translated into the other languages, okay?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, Major, before we really get going, I want to review with you your military service history and I'm going to simply read to you a summary of that history. And when I'm done you can tell meal if I've missed anything or if there is anything to be corrected we'll do so. Major, you joined the Royal Dutch Army in 1979 as a conscript and served as an NCO stationed at a variety of bases until 1991. Upon completing the officers' training school in 1993, you were commissioned as a Second Lieutenant and served with the 41st armoured infantry battalion where you trained the last company of conscripts. In 1994, you began your service with the 11th air mobile brigade, 13th Battalion, as an anti-tank platoon commander and subsequently served as deputy commanding officer of a company. From January through July of 1995, you served with DutchBat 3 as a fist Lieutenant during which time you were a patrol coordinator and intelligence officer in Charlie Company. Since your service in Bosnia you've served as brigade, battalion and corps level as chief of operational personal affairs, head of personnel and organisation, and deputy branch chief, personnel management. Those duties have involved preparing and forming missions abroad, such as various SFOR and KFOR missions and managing human resources related projects such as a headquarters reorganisation and implementing a new human resource application. And you also hold a degree in personnel policy and human resources. Major, does that accurately capture your service history?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, it's quite correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, in meeting with me, in preparation for your testimony, did you have an opportunity to review your prior testimony in the Krstic case?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, I had, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you in fact read every page of that testimony; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, I did, that's also correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you attest before the Trial Chamber that that testimony which you read was a faithful and accurate transcription of the testimony which you gave at the Krstic trial?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, it's also correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Major, what I'd like to do now is read to you a summary of your testimony in Krstic. It may take a little bit of time and I'm going to have to go a little bit slowly for the sake of the interpreters and I'd just ask to you listen carefully because I'll ask you if there were any changes or corrections that we need to make in my summary?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the other microphone for the witness please be switched on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I understand that the witness has switched it on himself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They are both on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Major.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: During the seven months then-Lieutenant Rutten served with DutchBat 3 he saw a decreasing -- he heard from the battalion that the Serbs were decreasing the movement of convoys by simply not giving them permission to go into the enclave. There was not enough food for the civilian population and the situation in the enclave became so bad that people would go through DutchBat's garbage when it was taken to the dump site looking for something edible. He identified a photograph he took while on patrol of civilians surrounding a truck which was dumping DutchBat garbage. Other DutchBat soldiers saw the same thing. On 10 July 1995, they heard severe impacts behind the compound from a rocket launcher based in Bratunac. Following the shelling they found an unexploded rocket just behind the compound. The shelling became heavier in the following days and stopped during the late evening. From their position near OP Papa the Serbs fired more or less in a lane on the Srebrenica-Potocari road and on or near DutchBat vehicles. There were no real military targets in Srebrenica or Potocari and his view of the purpose of the shelling was to intimidate DutchBat from leaving the compound and as a terror act. On Monday evening after the attack began, they heard from Bravo Company that the situation in Srebrenica was growing out of hand and that the refugees were on the move to Potocari. He then received an order to cut a hole in the rear side of the compound fence to let the refugees in, if necessary. Bravo Company soldiers arrived on the evening of 10 July with the first refugees who were kept at the bus Remise because he had not received an order permitting them on the compound and the fence had to be closed again. The only refugee brought to the compound was a heavily wounded woman taken to the battalion hospital. On Tuesday, 11 July, he was ordered to reopen the hole in the fence. Lieutenant Koster led a group of DutchBat soldiers at the bus Remise. At this time he, Lieutenant Rutten, heard that large groups of refugees were heading towards Potocari and that Bravo company had to leave Srebrenica because of the shelling and chaos there. The first groups of refugees began arriving at the rear side guided by Koster and his men at the bus Remise. Refugees arrived all day until approximately 5.00 or 6.00 in the evening, at which time he was ordered not to let in any more refugees because the factory hall itself was completely filled. He was then ordered by Major Otter at he shall to form three groups of ten men to secure the area of the bus remise where the refugees were. He then identified an area marked expression bus compound on an exhibit as the area to which he has referred as the bus remise and where he and his ten men remained on the night of 11 July. Lieutenants Koster and Schotman each also had ten men in the area. There were many refugees in that area and they placed white tape around the whole area as the only means available to make it clear that it was a secure area under UN surveillance. They also patrolled the area and the DutchBat doctor provided first aid. In the morning of 12 July 1995, small arms fire was followed by mortar fire and Serb soldiers set fire to house in the area near the location of the refugees. The first Serb soldiers to arrive were "more or less the Rambo types." He informed one of the of the Serb soldiers who looked like a leader that they could not cross the tape because it was UN territory and the refugees were under UN surveillance. But the Serb soldier and the rest with him just laughed and stepped over the tape and did as they pleased. Serb soldiers also stole equipment and personal items belonging to his men securing the bus compound. On 12 July, he saw General Mladic and his body guards arrive followed by a truck carrying bread and a fire truck with water. The distribution of the bread, water and candy was filmed. Immediately after the filming stopped, they also stopped handing out the bread, water, and candy. They even took back some of it from the refugees. He did not see the Serbs distribute anything else after that to the refugees on 12 or 13 July. Later on 12 July, as the buses were arriving, Serb soldiers threatened him to give up his weapon, flak vest and radio sets. He refused and told the soldiers that he needed to speak to their commander. Subsequently a Serb soldier who appeared to be a commander arrived, and again demanded his equipment while another Serb soldier grabbed his weapon. He again refused until the soldier pointed a gun at his head and demanded his radio set. He gave up one of his two sets then used the other to inform his superior officer that he had lost his weapon to the VRS. His men then also gave up their weapons and vests at gun point. He and his men were then taken to the bus compound and placed under guard of two Serb soldiers. He protested to a man he identified in an a photograph as Captain Mane that he was being held and that they had lost their equipment but Captain Mane sent him back to the rest of his group without looking at him. When Captain Mane returned a few hours later, Captain Mane sent him and his ten men, that is Lieutenant Rutten and his ten men escorted by two Serb soldiers, back to the compound where they spent the night. Also on 12 July, he saw a Serb soldier make a sign by running his finger across his throat at a man Lieutenant Rutten knew to be a Muslim soldier with a gunshot wound. On the morning of 13 July he was on duty in the operations room where he heard that Lieutenant Versteeg saw two buses loaded with men leave the vicinity of the "White House." He ordered Versteeg to follow the two buses because they were not leaving with the larger group of buses ready along the road. Versteeg followed the buss to Bratunac then radioed that the bus was not going to Kladanj but turned in another direction and that he was being obstructed by Serb soldiers from following the bus. He instructed Versteeg to follow the bus. Versteeg was unable to as the Serbs grabbed his car then hijacked it. Consequently they never learned where those buses went. Because of this incident with Versteeg, he decided to go to the "White House" himself under the pretext of delivering a wheelbarrow with packages of water and accompanied by a Sergeant Major. At the gate at the entrance to the "White House" he saw a huge pile of rucksacks and belongings. A few metres further were all kinds of identity cards and passports on the ground. The "White House" was well guarded by Serb soldiers who refused them entry. Also in front of the house were two Dutch corporals who had been given Lieutenant stars so the Serbs would think they were of higher rank. He and the Sergeant Major then entered the left rear area of the house which was actually two houses under one roof. There they saw photographs of men laid out in every room, which were empty. They exited that area and tried to look around an orchard area behind the house but were prevented at gun point by two Serb soldiers. They returned to the entrance and were able to enter after offering Serb soldiers some water. Once inside, he saw a Muslim man hanging from the staircase by one arm so he asked a Serb soldier to lower him so that his feet could touch the ground. While this was being done he tried to enter a room on the right side from which he had heard voices but was prevented whether a Serb soldier in a green camouflage uniform put his gun in his face and eventually stuck it in his mouth. He then stepped outside and saw a Serb soldier at the gate telling men arriving at the house to throw down their things and, a few metres later, telling them to throw their identity cards. While the Sergeant Major stayed at the staircase, Lieutenant Rutten went back inside and upstairs where he found two rooms filled with 50 men and boys from age 12 to 55. He photographed both groups of men but will to stop because a Serb soldier was arriving with more men. They then left the house. It was clear to him that this was no normal interrogation as normal procedure with POWs would require a system of identifying the prisoners whereas it was very clear to him that the men in the "White House" would not need their IDs or belongings. Later that evening the Serbs set fire to the belongings and IDs which were outside the house. The fire burned for two days. He identified a photograph he took of the smoke rising from the fire. He did not see any signs of violence or torture during the times he visited the "White House." After leaving the "White House," he went to the area where Lieutenant van Duijn was posted with a blockade of four APCs. At that location a local interpreter informed him that there were rumours that men had been killed near a well near the road on the Budak side. He, Sergeant Major van Schaik, and Koster then passed through the APC blockade and followed a dirt road. They saw a woman who made a sign along her throat and pointed further up the road. In a very bushy area they found a small stream on the left behind a house near a meadow. As soon as they saw the meadow, they saw some bodies lying along the stream. He inspected the bodies, which were nine men in civilian clothes lying with their faces toward the stream. Two were on their sides. All had small-calibre gun shots to their backs at heart level. The men were approximately 45 to 55 years old. He touched the bodies which were warm. The blood was still running and there were no flies on them. They had not been shot long before. He told van Schaik to pick up the identification that was on the grass in front of the bodies and he took a photograph of Koster kneeling between the bodies. He also photographed all nine bodies. At that point there was firing at them. After the first shot, he saw a woman running out of one of the houses in the area chased by a Serb soldier. He told van Schaik to drop all of the identification which he had picked up and that they had to leave. They heard more shooting nearby and reached the dirt road. At the blockade they grabbed a stretcher so it would look like they were helping some refugees. He reported what he had seen to Lieutenant Colonel Karremans who told him that he would pass his report on to a higher level. He then remained at the blockade where he took some pictures of what the Serbs were doing and observed a DutchBat Lieutenant and some DutchBat soldiers actually assisting the deportation of the Muslims though trying to do their best to help the refugees. Looking through the camera it would not give too good an idea of what the UN was doing there. The situation was that DutchBat personnel had taped an area where about 60 to 70 people could be placed who were then directed to the buses. Behind another line were standing all of the rest of the refugees who were being helped and given water by other DutchBat soldiers. Because there were Serb soldiers sitting all along the road with their weapons, DutchBat was more or less helping with the deportation and not an impartial party any more. He told this to van Duijn who had a different point of view. On the other side of the line at the buses, Serb soldiers were carrying out the separation of the men from their families. UN soldiers were not working with the refugees at the point where the men were being separated from the women. When he returned to Holland he turned his film over to someone from the army's intelligence branch but was later informed that something had happened during its development. He was then ordered by his company commander to escort the last bus that is were leaving. He and his driver prepared a jeep and parked it next to the compound entrance while waiting for the last buses to leave. As they waited, he told his driver to accompany him back to the "White House" so that he could have as many witnesses as possible. By that time, the pile of belongings was huge and many more IDs and passports were laying on the ground. They went to the previously empty left side of the house and saw two Serb soldiers on the staircase which was filled with Muslim men. He could see the total fear on the faces of the men and boys and, though he never thought that it really existed, he could even smell death there because it was total fear. Serb soldiers in green camouflage uniforms were taking deutschmarks from Muslims at gun point. They walked back to the front of the house and saw the balcony totally filled with men and boys. They went to the right side of the house but could not get in. He estimates that almost 300 men were in the house and on the balcony. It was completely filled up. The two Dutch soldiers who were still posted in front of the house also said that it was completely filled. He then spoke with a Dutch Major and Warrant Officer Rave about getting the men out of the house. Rave and Major Kingori then spoke to the Serbs at the "White House" and sometime later buses arrived to take the men away. He could not escort the buses because he had to wait to escort the last buses and no one else could escort them because all of the soldiers who had tried to escort the convoys had been thrown out or their jeeps hijacked by the Serbs. It was no use to escort the buses when they lost all their materiel and were brought back to the compound half an hour or a day later. The escort had not succeeded at all. During his second visit to the "White House," he saw a man whom he identified as being on the left-hand side of Exhibit 28/8.1, which is a photograph depicting two males, one of whom is wearing a T-shirt and facing the camera. He saw this man, who did not look like a plain soldier, speaking to all of the Serb soldiers who came to the "White House," including soldiers in black uniforms who arrived in private cars that stopped in front of the "White House." Some of these cars arrived from Srebrenica and others from Potocari. Their occupants spoke to this man before driving away. By the time it was clear that the last buses were filled up, later in the day on 13 July, the battalion had stopped escorting the convoys because it was no use any more. He asked his company ops room if he could make an attempt to escort the last buses and was given the okay. So he quickly drove to the head of the convoy which was heading toward OP Papa. After driving approximately a kilometre to a kilometre and a half in Potocari, a private car containing three Serb soldiers in green camouflage uniforms came up behind them. Next another car containing two Serb soldiers came from the side of the road and blocked the road. The soldiers were pointing weapons at them. The actions of the two cars appeared well organised. At his instruction, his driver then made a U-turn and returned to the compound. As a result, the convoy was not escorted. When he returned to the compound he was told to accompany a truck and some medical personnel who were going into Srebrenica to pick up the last elderly people left behind or along the road. Enroute he was stopped by Serb soldiers who ordered him, his driver and a Sergeant in the back seat out at gun point. The Serb soldiers told them that they would have to continue on in the truck. When they reached the Bravo Company compound, he saw Serb looting the compound and driving Dutch APCs filled with stolen material. The Serbs had also emptied the weapons collection point. Along the road they found a few elderly people whom the medical personnel treated and placed in the truck. From what he saw, the Serb soldiers who were in command only had to say things once and everyone understood what he or what the senior commander meant, so you could easily tell who was in control. The Serbs knew exactly who was in charge on the Dutch side and more or less always addressed the Lieutenants who were around. They asked him for his rank and did not speak to the soldiers. When he was threatened by Serb soldiers as he was gathering information he considered the threats serious and his life could be in danger if he did his job.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, Major, that concludes the summary. Are there any corrections or additions as you sat there and listened to it that you'd care to make?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: No, there are not, no corrections.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I want to turn your attention in the time we have left to a handful of areas that arise from your prior testimony, and the first is that you testified that during your seven months with DutchBat 3, you experienced a decreasing number of UNHCR convoys. Do you recall when that decrease began?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: The decrease began the end of February and the beginning of March and it was a -- an intense decrease because we also got the news that the warehouse in Srebrenica itself, where everything was assembled together, all goods was getting more and more lower on stock.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how about the DutchBat resupply convoys? Did they experience a decrease as well?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time, more or less, we were also on minimise. In fact the previous battalion from DutchBat 2 was also on minimise when we came in but it became more and more severe also the beginning of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I want to turn your attention briefly to the actual VRS attack on the enclave. Did you have an opportunity to see what was being struck by the shelling?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes. Warehouses around the compound itself, what was in our line of sight and it warehouses near for instance Budak hill that was on the opposite of the compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you say compound you're referring to the Potocari compound?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, I'm referring to the Potocari compound, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you also testified about the VRS firing along a lane on the Potocari-Srebrenica road. And that that firing was on or near DutchBat vehicles. Do you have any specific examples of such firing on or near DutchBat vehicles that you can tell the Trial Chamber about?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes. There were more but one specific it was from the hills above OP Papa, it was on a map on the JNA map the hills of Purici, they had their different kinds of weapons there and they shot in a lane towards Potocari, specific -- yeah, something that could even laugh about it later, at least I did, is a story about a colleague, Major Boering, who was in the S5 team came in driving and was shot at with his -- when he came driving in with his jeep and I said to him -- and he was driving quite fast. And I said to him when he came into the building, "Are you always driving that fast?" And he couldn't see that as a joke but that is an example what really happened when every car or every vehicle that came out of Kadin [phoen] was fired at.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, I want to turn your attention now and ask you a couple of questions regarding the several hours during which you were being held by the Serb soldiers after they had taken your weapons and some of your equipment as well. Now, after DutchBat withdrew on 21 July, you spent a couple of days in Zagreb before returning to Holland; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And while in Zagreb, do you recall completing an ICTY, UN peace keeper interview questionnaire?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, it's also correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in that questionnaire, you were asked a series of questions related to whether or not you had been captured or subject to restriction on your freedom of movement, do you remember those questions?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, they were in the same as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: One of those questions was can you identify the military/paramilitary/police or other personnel taking you hostage. Do you recall what your answer was to that question as you sit here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. What's the objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: I hate to interrupt my learned friend. I would just like a specific reference to the date thereof questionnaire and the page number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I that I that can be handled by Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour and I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's a fair intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That is an undated questionnaire. The -- it is on the second page of the document but it's listed on our exhibit list as I believe UN peacekeeper interview questionnaire, the ERN at the top is 00565014 and I believe it is also the second page of the B/C/S translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, Major, do you remember what your answer was to that question?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes. I spoke to several soldiers and tried to make at least as a normal contact and they had they told me that they were from a special unit from Belgrade and special police unit, they said, because I couldn't identify any symbols or insignia on the uniform. It was a quite normal conversation. We spoke about how they came there and asked me also where -- where I was from in Holland and so on, so to me it seemed a very normal conversation with a true and honest belief to it, to what they said at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You referred to the uniforms. Do you recall anything in particular about the actual uniform?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes. There was a difference because they didn't wear any flak vests, the most of them. Some of them had and this special police unit had that were light blue flak jackets and they were very interested about ours because we had our -- and they called it "pancir." Our flak vests were more protective than the ones they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: How about the rest of the uniforms, do you recall anything particular about the appearance of those?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: They were also the camouflage uniforms, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, what -- in what language were you conducting this conversation?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: It was -- they were not that good on English but they spoke in mostly in German with some words Serbo-Croatian in between but in German they managed quite well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So when you use the term here special police, is that your term or is that the term that the soldiers used when you were speaking with them?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: No. They used the term "Specijalni," and that means such as Special Forces, not the Special Forces that the word that we use in the army then we mean Special Forces commandos and so on but they were special police force, a force, especially with a special task that they said to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what if anything did they tell you about their relationship with the army?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: They didn't tell nothing much about that. They didn't go in detail to that. At least, as I tried they weren't giving any answers to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, I want to turn your attention to the nine bodies. With respect to those nine bodies you discovered, you testified that you observed identification documents scattered around those bodies. Can you describe those documents with any detail for the Trial Chamber, please?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes. Well, all kinds of identity cards. We hadn't that much time to review them specific but I saw them earlier used in the enclave, a kind of working permit, small cards, with sometimes with pass photos on it and all kinds of papers were lying around those bodies, also including some passports.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So specifically with respect to these documents that you saw around the bodies, did any of them bear photographs?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, they did, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And from what you saw, Major, did you observe any evidence that the bodies had been moved from one location to the other?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: No, there were no traces of that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Any blood trails, for example, anything like that?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. They were shot on spot there and were never moved.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I want to turn your attention to your contact with Lieutenant van Duijn. You testified that you and then Lieutenant van Duijn had had a difference of opinion as to the appearance and what you perceived to be the consequences of his actions at the APC blockade on 13 July. Now, was there anything in particular about the separation process which you saw that gave rise to your response or your opposition to what you saw Lieutenant van Duijn doing?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Lieutenant van Duijn was at a certain spot and I was more around, and I saw more in detail what happened around the compound and I was also along the line of buses so I could easier see also in the neighbourhood of the "White House" what had happened over there, and to my opinion he wasn't quite aware of what was really happening as a result of his actions near to those four APCs. So there was a difference in opinion. And I was behind those APCs making some photos and, yeah, if you look into a camera, it's, yeah, you see a different picture, a narrow picture, and then, yeah, looking -- it didn't look that good to me so that was the reason that I picked out the discussion with Lieutenant van Duijn.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you referred to a long line of buses. Was there anything going on along that line of buses which contributed to your opposition or response to what Lieutenant van Duijn was doing?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: In fact, he was assembling groups or helping with it and the moment the groups, the line was lowered, the group started moving to the buses, and it was on the front side so on the compound side that these moved but at the back side of the buses where the houses were and also where also that "White House," was there were all along that line Serb soldiers and that it was not in the line of sight of Lieutenant van Duijn so at that line, easily men and boys could pick -- pick out of the line and were brought or sent to the houses directed by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you refer to the line are you referring to the line of buses?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, I'm referring to the line of buss.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you actually see men or boys being separated out by those soldiers that were along that line of buses?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I actually saw that, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, when we met first a couple of weeks ago do you recall that I showed you an aerial photograph of the Potocari base?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And at that time, did that photo have any names of any buildings or landmarks marked on it already or did you identify those for me from your memory at that time?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: It was a photograph with no identification on it and I marked them out again to clear the picture again, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you did that with little stickies that you placed?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, the yellow stickers, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did I also ask you to trace the route that you took to the location where you discovered the nine bodies?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you did that without actually marking the exhibit, just showing me with ...

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: With a pencil.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, did I subsequently show you a similar aerial photograph of the Potocari base which you yourself had marked during your testimony in the Krstic trial?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, you also did.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you remember that you were asked to mark -- let me withdraw that question. Do you remember what you were asked to mark during the Krstic trial on that exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what was that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: That was the spot of the -- where I found that nine bodies, yeah.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could you please make a pause because of overlap, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm receiving a message from the interpreters. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Please comply.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: In addition to the spot, Major, did you also indicate the route on that exhibit that you took to that?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Group of bodies?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: It's also marked out, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you compared the route that you had traced for me with the route that you showed in Krstic, how were they in terms of their similarity or lack of similarity?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: To me they were exactly the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: At this time, if we could be shown 65 ter 1522, please? Or P02179. Either way. Do you have an image on your screen, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, I have the image, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what is that document, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: That document is the place where I marked the route and the place where I found the bodies and this is the situation that I found in 1995, July 1995, and also marked this one out in the Krstic case. It's the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in some of your prior statements and on the sketch you drew in connection with the so-called Kodak team investigation, you referred to a location where you saw Muslim men being taken on the first day of the transportations. Do you know or can you tell the Trial Chamber what that general area or location was called on the first day of the transportations?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: It were the houses what you see between the yellow line there and also already the "White House," it's in the opposite of the compound?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, focusing your attention to the 12th, you referred to two houses?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Was that near an area that went by any other name?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes. That was the area of the car wash, the blue -- a blue building, yeah; it was a former car wash.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If you would with Madam Usher's assistance just take the stylus that's next to the --

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Okay. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Would you just circle the area you're referring to as the car wash and just write "car wash" next to that?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if you would identify the two houses that you referred to where you saw Muslim men being taken on the first day of the transportations, and if you would just next to that write, "First day"?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, would you please mark the area where you were held by the special police soldiers with an A?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Again, keeping your attention on the 12th of July, can you just mark with small letter Rs the areas where the refugees were located on the 12th?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how about in relation to the -- let me ask you first question. On this photograph, can you identify the area where those four APCs that you referred to are located and if you could just write APCs next to that?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And on the 12th, can you mark again with some small Rs where the refugees were who were waiting to pass through that blockade as we have referred to it were located?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: This is the line of of the refugees here?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: On the 12th, how far back did that line extend?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: It was almost along the road. It's here, it's almost -- this whole area was packed until the APCs -- the line behind the APC.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: For the record describing a rectangular area emanating from a circle in the centre of an image at the top of which is a letter R.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I see that we are right up against the break, Your Honour. I think we'll have to initial this and save it and then work with it a little bit more tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. You need to put your signature top right-hand corner, please. You can write it with the stylus.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have just a few more questions. I should be able to finish in five to ten minutes tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can't overstay because we will be keeping the other Trial Chamber starting on time. Major, we won't finish tomorrow and Friday we are not sitting, so that means we will continue and finish with you on Monday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much for everything and.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, it is important that between now and tomorrow and then after tomorrow until Monday, you do not communicate or let anyone communicate with you in relation to the matters that you are testifying upon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. We stand adjourned until tomorrow morning at 9.00. That's it. Thank you.
